facts: The **$x$-intercepts** are the points where the curve meets the horizontal axis, including where it touches it, written as points such as $(3,0)$.
The **$y$-intercept** is the one point where the curve meets the vertical axis.
The **axis of symmetry** is a vertical line, so it is written as an equation such as $x=3$.
The **vertex** is a point on the curve, written as a pair such as $(3,-4)$, and it lies on the axis of symmetry.
When there are two distinct $x$-intercepts, the axis of symmetry passes exactly midway between them. Otherwise, read the vertex: the axis passes vertically through it.
A concave-up parabola has a minimum and a concave-down parabola has a maximum.
The maximum or minimum **value** is the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, not the whole point.
A parabola can have two, one or no $x$-intercepts, but it always has exactly one $y$-intercept.
steps: Read the $x$-intercepts and the $y$-intercept where the curve meets each axis, including where it touches an axis.
If there are two distinct $x$-intercepts, find the axis of symmetry midway between them; otherwise, use the vertical line through the vertex. Write the axis as an equation.
Read the vertex as a point and state whether it is a maximum or a minimum.

The axis of symmetry is $x=-2$.

The parabola is concave up, so its lowest point is the vertex $(0,-2)$.
The minimum value is the $y$-coordinate of that point.
The minimum value is $y=-2$.
